title: FA/84/2015 of Agra Diocesan Trust Association AND ANOTHER Vs Rajan Peter Singh AND OTHERS

paras.text:
Reserved Judgment
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
First Appeal no. 84 of 2015
Agra Diocesan Trust Asson. & another ....... Appellants
Versus
Rajan Peter and others ....... Respondents
Mr. V.K. Kohli, Senior Advocate assisted by Mr. Kanti Ram Sharma,
Advocate for the appellants.
Mr. Santosh Kumar and Mr. Sanjay Bhatt, Advocates for respondent no. 2.
Mr. Nikhil Singhal, Advocate for respondent no. 5.
Chronological list of cases referred:
 1. (2019) 2 SCC 338, Chairman, Board of Trustees, Sri Ram Mandir
 Jagtial Karimnagar District Andhra Pradesh Vs S. Rajyalaxmi
 (dead) and others,
2. (2016) 16 SCC 483, Rakesh Mohindra Vs Anita Beri and others
 3. (2008) 4 SCC 594, Anathula Sudhakar Vs P. Buchi Reddy (Dead)
 by LRs. and others,
 4. AIR 2007 SUPREME COURT 1721, Smt. J. Yashoda Vs Smt. K.
 Shobha Rani
5. (2006) 3 SCC 312, Kishore Kumar Khaitan and another Vs
Praveen Kumar Singh
6. (1975) 4 SCC 664, Ashok Dulichand Vs Madahavlal Dube &
another.

[Per: Hon'ble Lok Pal Singh, J.]
 Present First Appeal has been preferred
by the appellants against the judgment and decree
dated 30.03.2015 passed by the Additional District
Judge, Vikasnagar, whereby the suit filed by the
appellant / plaintiff was dismissed.
2) Facts leading to filing of present appeal
are that plaintiff no. 1, Agra Diocesan Trust
Association (hereinafter referred to as 'ADTA') is a
charitable and religious company duly incorporated
under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956,

2
having its registered office at 4/166-B, Church
Road, Civil Lines, Agra. Mr. N. Munawar is the
Secretary of ADTA. The Diocese of Agra, Church of
North India, plaintiff no. 2, is a religious Institution.
The Diocese of Agra is one of the Dioceses of the
Church of North India and functions for and on
behalf of the Church of North India under its
constitution and bye-laws within the territorial
jurisdiction consisting of several civil districts in
western Uttar Pradesh. The details of such
properties is detailed in the Schedule attached to
the plaint. Revd. Prem Prakash Habil is the
Secretary of Diocese of Agra.
3) The Lucknow Diocesan Trust Association
(hereinafter referred as 'LDTA') is also a charitable
and religious company, incorporated in the year
1924 under the Indian Companies Act of 1913
having its registered office at 6, Sarojini Naidu
Marg, Allahabad, U.P.
4) As per plaint averments, the Church of
England was propagating Christianity in India
during the British era, where it was known as
Church of England in India. The Church of
England in India was subsequently known as
Church of India, Burma and Ceylon (CIBC). On
formation of Pakistan, it was known as Church of
India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon (CIPBC). There
was only Church of England, Church of England in
India and CIPBC, but there was no church in the
name of Anglican Church. It is averred that on the
union and amalgamation of six Uniting Churches,

3
Church of North India (CNI) was formed and
inaugurated on 29.11.1970:
 i) The council of Baptist Churches in Northern
India.
 ii) The Church of Brethren in India.
 iii) The Church of India, Pakistan, Burma and
Ceylon,
 iv) The Disciples of Christ,
 v) The Methodist Church (British & Australian
Conferences)
 vi) The United Church of Northern India.
5) It is further averred that several
properties, owned by the Church Missionary Trust
Association Ltd. London (CMTA) in India for benefit
of the Church of India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon
one of the uniting churches. CMTA entrusted its
properties within the Diocesan of Lucknow to LDTA
through registered Trust Deed dated 24.12.1952 for
management, control and owning the said
properties for the benefit of the Church of India,
Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon or any other body of
church or association by which in future it may be
designated. It is also averred that the merger and
unification of above mentioned 6 churches into CNI
was upheld by the Hon'ble High Court of Bombay in
Company Appeal no 1211 / 1998, Advocate Nitin
Mahadeo Pawar and others Vs United Church of
Northern India Trust Association vide judgment
dated 19.01.1999. The Hon'ble Apex Court also
rejected the appeal against the said decision in
1999. The above listed Churches merged and
became known as Church of North India (CNI) and
all the properties, ecclesiastical or otherwise vested
in and became the properties of Church of North
India. The Church of North India adopted its

4
constitution at the ordinary Synod of the Church of
North India on 9-13 July, 1974. As per said
Constitution, CNI is divided into several Diocese on
territorial basis. In part II Chapter III Clause I of
the said Constitution defines the Diocese. The
Diocese of Lucknow is one of the Diocese of CNI. As
per the constitution of CNI, Synod can divide the
existing Diocese in new Diocese. The Diocese of
Lucknow made a request to the Synod of CNI on
21.08.1973 to divide Diocese of Lucknow and the
Western part of the U.P. was divided forming
Diocese of Agra in 1976. The Diocesan Council of
the Diocese of Agra held its first meeting on
09.04.1976.
6) It is also averred that the Diocesan
Council of the Lucknow Diocese made the
recommendation dated 21.08.1973 to the Executive
Committee of the Synod of the CNI for its division
into two i.e. Diocese of Lucknow and Diocese of
Agra, covering the defined territory mainly western
part of the then Uttar Pradesh coming under
Diocese of Agra and Eastern part of the then U.P.
coming under the Diocese of Lucknow. The said
proposal of the Lucknow Diocese (unit of CNI) was
approved by the Executive Committee of the Synod
of the CNI and on its decision, the Diocese of Agra
came into existence in the year 1976.
Subsequently, on 09.04.1976, the first meeting of
the Diocesan Council of the Diocese of Agra was
held and from that date as per the constitution of
CNI referred above, both Diocese of Lucknow and
LDTA effectively divested all their rights, duties,

5
functions, liabilities, assets etc. and vested
beneficial ownership into the Diocese of Agra till a
charitable company was incorporated in October
1988 with the approval of Executive Committee of
the CNI Synod, which is the plaintiff no. 1
Company, i.e, ADTA.
7) The head of the Diocese, the Bishop, is
also the Chairman of the Charitable Company.
Thus, the Bishop of the Diocese of Agra is Chairman
of ADTA plaintiff no. 1. The Bishop is appointed by
CNI. In this manner the Diocese of Agra have
effective control over ADTA and the Diocese being
unit of CNI is under control and management of
CNI. As per the Articles of Association of the ADTA
and the LDTA the membership of both the said
companies constitutes from the members of
respective Diocesan Council. In this manner, each
Diocese (unit of CNI) i.e. Diocese of Agra and
Diocese of Lucknow have effective control over
ADTA & LDTA respectively, and Diocese being Unit
of CNI, is under control and management of CNI. It
is averred that Diocese of Agra and Diocese of
Lucknow have well defined jurisdiction i.e. territory
respectively and can legally function within their
territory only and not beyond. Para 2, Chapter III
Section IV Clause 2 of the CNI constitution provides
that the number of Diocese and their boundaries
shall be determined by the Synod. Chapter III,
Section IV, Clause 5 of the CNI constitution
provides that every Diocese while exercising
autonomous power and function of administration
within its territory is an integral part of the CNI. So

6
that ADTA, the LDTA their respective Diocese of
Agra and Diocese of Lucknow all exist and work for
CNI only, who owns and manage the properties in
their jurisdiction as sole beneficiary. In Part III,
Chapter 2 of the said Constitution, the Rules
relating to division of the Diocese have been framed.
It is averred that on creation of Diocese of Agra by
division of Diocese of Lucknow in 1976, all the
properties and all the rights of LDTA in the territory
of Diocese of Agra with respect to the property
situated in the said territory passed on to Diocese of
Agra as beneficial owner through ADTA (plaintiff no.
1).
8) It is alleged that the LDTA after creation
of the Diocese of Agra cannot operate or exercise
any right whatsoever in the territory of the Diocese
of Agra and cannot realize the income from all the
properties in the Diocese of Agra which is meant for
the exclusive benefit of the Diocese of Agra. The
LDTA has also no right or obligation to discharge
the said function of the CNI in the territory of the
Diocese of Agra earlier discharged by it in undivided
Diocese of Lucknow. So all the funds / income
accruing from the said properties i.e. within
territory of Diocese of Agra, were and are given to
the Diocese of Agra, through ADTA. It is averred
that the Power of Attorney executed on 15.07.1977
and 30.01.1993 are basically not a document
creating an ordinary relationship between the
principal and the agent but on the contrary the
spirit behind it is to implement the provisions of
constitution of CNI i.e. one Diocese does not have

7
any right / jurisdiction to exercise in the territory of
other Diocese. In order to put the division of right
between Diocese of Agra and Diocese of Lucknow
this Power of Attorney was executed by LDTA and so
this Attorney is not only the irrevocable power of
attorney but also a document of 'cessation' between
the two Dioceses and after this document LDTA
forever and for all purposes have no concern with
any properties for anything, within the territory of
Diocese of Agra. Moreover, even the Schedule at the
end of the said Power of Attorney mentioned that
the properties situated within the territory of
Diocese of Agra are exclusively for the benefit and
purpose of Diocese of Agra. It is alleged that LDTA
is not entitled to sell or transfer or for any income /
consideration amount accruing / arising from said
properties whether by sale or otherwise. It is
further alleged that defendant no. 1 is posing
himself as the Secretary of defendant no. 2, the
body which does not exist and has entered into an
agreement with defendant no. 3 to 5 on 27.02.2005.
It is also alleged that the defendants have no
authority, interest and right of any kind in the
property within the Diocese of Agra over which the
plaintiffs alone have all the rights. Defendant no. 1
has no right to interfere in the possession and
management of property and attempting to sell and
transfer the properties of the plaintiffs illegally and
without any right or authority. Defendant no. 1 has
already entered into an agreement as mentioned
above. It is apprehended that there is every
possibility that defendant nos. 1 and 2 may transfer
the properties of the plaintiffs and if they succeed in

8
their evil designs, the valuable properties of
religious and charitable institution will be illegally
sold and misappropriated. It is averred that cause
of action for the suit arose on 27.02.2005 when
defendant nos. 1 and 2 entered into an agreement
with defendant nos. 3 to 5 for the transfer of the
property described at the end of the Schedule of this
plaint.
9) With the averments as above, the
Plaintiffs / appellants Agra Diocesan Trust
Association filed a suit against the defendants /
respondents seeking a decree for permanent
injunction restraining the defendants, their agents,
servants, successors and assignees from causing
any interference in the possession, control and
management of the plaintiff in respect of the
property described in Schedule A and B of the plaint
or transferring, alienating, mortgaging or creating
any third party charge on the suit property.
10) In a nutshell, the plaintiffs claim that
initially LDTA was the owner of the property in
question. By means of a resolution, the property
fell in the territorial jurisdiction of ADTA, came into
the share of the plaintiff wherefor no title has been
annexed by the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs in
paragraph 17 of the plaint have stated that the
LDTA is not entitled to sell or transfer or for any
income / consideration amount accruing / arising
from said properties whether by sale or otherwise.

9
11) It is pertinent to mention here that the
plaintiffs have not impleaded LDTA as party
defendant, though they claim that the property in
question came to the plaintiffs from LDTA. In so far
as defendant no. 1 / respondent no. 1 is concerned,
the defendant no. 1 has claimed himself as
Secretary of the LDTA. Be that as it may, the fact
remains that LDTA was not impleaded as party
defendant wherefor the plaintiffs claimed that the
property came to them from the LDTA. It depicts
from the perusal of the suit property that the suit
property is agriculture property.
12) Defendant no. 1 filed his written
statement and contended that LDTA came into
existence in the year 1952 and that LDTA being the
owner of the property in dispute and he being the
Secretary LDTA has the right to execute the
agreement to sell in favour of respondent nos. 3 to
5. Plaintiffs are not in possession over the suit
property, as such, there is no question of giving
threat to them by the defendant no. 1. In the
additional statements, it is stated that the property
in question is the property of Church Missionary
Trust Association Ltd., which has been transferred
to LDTA through a registered trust deed vide
resolution dated 15.10.1952 and at present LDTA is
the owner-in-possession of the property in question
and all the right and title are vested with LDTA. It
is also stated that ADTA and Diocese of Agra,
Church of North India have no right or interest in
the property in question. Lastly, it is stated that the
suit filed by the plaintiffs is not maintainable.

10
13) Defendant nos. 3 to 5 also filed their
written statement. It was admitted that defendant
no. 1 is the Secretary of defendant no. 2 and that an
agreement to sell dated 27.02.2005 was executed
between defendant nos. 1 & 2 and defendant nos. 3
to 5. It is stated that the relief sought by the
plaintiffs cannot be granted to them as the
averments made in the plaint are false. In the
additional statement, it is stated that pursuant to
the agreement to sell dated 27.02.2005, an advance
of Rs.35,00,000/- against the total sale
consideration of Rs. 1,25,00,000/- was paid.
14) On behalf of the plaintiffs, Sushil Kumar,
was examined as PW1. No witness was examined
on behalf of defendants.

15) On the basis of pleadings of the parties,
the trial court framed following issues:
 i) Whether the plaintiffs are owner in
possession of the property in dispute?
ii) To what reliefs, the plaintiffs are entitled?
16) The trial court dismissed the suit of the
plaintiffs vide judgment and decree dated
30.03.2015. The suit was dismissed, firstly, on the
ground that it has not been disclosed whether the
property in dispute is the same property which is
mentioned in the deed dated 25.10.2008 executed
between the Directors, Chairman and Secretary of
LDTA and the Directors, Chairman and Secretary of
ADTA. The second ground was that the property in
question prior to execution of deed dated

11
25.10.2008 was recorded in the name of LDTA. It
has not been proved that after execution of deed
dated 25.10.2008 the name of ADTA was ever
recorded in the name of plaintiff and whether they
are in possession of the property which is the same
property and also that the land in question is an
agricultural land, hence court has no jurisdiction to
try the suit.
17) I have heard learned counsel for the
parties and perused the material brought on record.
18) The sole point of determination to be
considered by this Court is as under:
Whether the plaintiffs are owner in possession
of the suit property?

19) Mr. V.K. Kohli, learned Senior counsel
appearing on behalf of the plaintiffs / appellants
vehemently argued that pursuant to the agreement
dated 27.02.2005, sale deed has been executed by
defendant no. 1 in favour of defendant nos. 3 to 5
and for that a separate suit has been instituted by
the plaintiffs. Learned Senior Counsel would
submit that defendant no. 1 has executed the sale
deed without any authority of law. He would
further submit that the learned trial court has erred
in law in recording the findings that the property in
question prior to execution of Trust deed dated
25.10.2008 was recorded in the name of LDTA and
it has not been proved that after execution of said
deed, the name of ADTA was ever recorded in the

12
name of plaintiffs, and whether they are in
possession of the property which is the same
property, as also a further finding that the land in
question is an agricultural land, as such, trial court
has no jurisdiction to try the suit. Learned counsel
for the appellants would submit that no such
defence taken by the respondents in their pleadings
and also there was no such issue framed by the
court below as to whether the property mentioned
in the Schedule of the plaint is different from the
property mentioned in the Trust deed dated
25.10.2008 or was it an agricultural land. He
would further submit that mere execution of an
agreement to sell in favour of respondent nos. 3 to 5
does not confer any right or title in favour of
respondent nos. 3 to 5. It is contended that full
details of the property in dispute for which
injunction has been sought has been mentioned in
the Schedule mentioned in the plaint and the
plaintiffs have specifically sought injunction in
respect of the properties described in the schedule
of the plaint. It is also contended that defendant
no. 1 in his written statement has merely stated
that he has right to sell the property in question. In
paragraph no. 27 of his written statement,
defendant no. 1 has further stated that the property
in question was transferred to LDTA in the year
1952. On the other hand, plaintiffs submitted that
the properties which were under the
management of LDTA were divided into two
dioceses and the property in question came to the
share of ADTA. It is urged that as no evidence
was filed on behalf of defendant no. 1, neither he

13
appeared in the witness box, hence the case of the
plaintiff remained unrebutted.
20) Learned senior counsel would further
urge that so far as defendant no. 2 is concerned, it
does not exist at all. So far as defendant nos. 3 to 5
are concerned they did not get any right on the
execution of an agreement to sell executed in their
favour. The defence taken on behalf of respondent
nos. 5/1 to 5/3 was that the agreement to sell was
executed by defendant no. 1 in their favour and
plaintiffs have no concern with the agreement to sell
executed in their favour. It is contended that
plaintiff has a concern in the matter that their
possession should not be disturbed. The case of the
plaintiffs was that the immoveable property can
only be transferred by sale. It is contended that the
court below has failed to consider the fact that it
was a trust property and by resolution the
management of the properties were bifurcated
between LDTA and ADTA and the property in
dispute was vested with ADTA for the purpose of
management. Lastly, it was argued that the
judgment and decree dated 30.03.2015, passed by
the court below is illegal, perverse, against the
pleadings and evidence on record and the same is
liable to be set aside and the suit of the plaintiffs
deserves to be allowed.
21) Learned counsel for the respondent nos.
5/1 to 5/3 argued that the burden of proof to prove
ownership and possession lies on the plaintiff and
also on the point that a suit for injunction, without

14
any averment in respect of possession over the suit
property on the date of filing of suit, is not
maintainable. He placed reliance on the following
judgments in support of his contention:
 i) Chairman, Board of Trustees, Sri Ram
Mandir Jagtial Karimnagar District Andhra
Pradesh Vs S. Rajyalaxmi (dead) and others,
(2019) 2 SCC 338
ii) Kishore Kumar Khaitan and another Vs
Praveen Kumar Singh, (2006) 3 SCC 312
22) In the case of Sri Ram Mandir1, their
Lordships of Hon'ble Apex Court have held in
paragraph nos. 21 and 22 as under:
 "21. It is an established position of law that,
the burden to prove ownership over the suit
property is on the plaintiffs. This Court in Parimal
Vs Veena, (2011) 3 SCC 545, held that:
 "19. The provisions of Section 101 of
the Evidence Act provide that the burden of
proof of the facts rests on the party who
substantially asserts it and not on the party
who denies it. In fact, burden of proof
means that a party has to prove an
allegation before he is entitled to a judgment
in his favour. Section 103 provides that the
burden of proof as to any particular fact lies
on that person who wishes the court to
believe in its existence, unless it is provided
by any special law that the proof of that fact
shall lie on any particular person. The
provision of Section 103 amplifies the
general rule of Section 101 that the burden
of proof lies on the person who asserts the
affirmative of the facts in issue."
(emphasis supplied)
 22. In the present case, the respondent-plaintiffs failed to discharge their burden of proof
by being unable to furnish necessary documentary
and oral evidence to prove their claim. But, the
High Court without appreciating the aforesaid
evidence and claims made by the appellant
(Defendant 4), decreed the suit in favour of the
respondents-plaintiffs by solely relying on the
entry made in the book of the Endowments

15
Department stating the boundaries of the temple.
The aforesaid judgment of the High Court is
untenable in law as it is based on erroneous
appreciation of evidence."
23) In paragraph nos. 6 and 7 of the
judgment rendered by Hon'ble Apex Court in
Kishore Kumar Khaitan5 case, it has been held as
under:
"6. An interim mandatory injunction is not
a remedy that is easily granted. It is an order that
is passed only in circumstances which are clear
and the prima facie materials clearly justify a
finding that the status quo has been altered by
one of the parties to the litigation and the interests
of justice demanded that the status quo ante be
restored by way of an interim mandatory
injunction. Keeping this principle in mind, it is
necessary to see whether in the case on hand, the
Additional District Judge was justified in passing
the interim order of injunction.
7. Admittedly, the defendants are the
owners of the building. The plaintiff was setting
up a case that the plaint schedule part of the
building had been granted to him on lease on
17.04.1998 and that he had obtained possession
thereof on the basis of such a lease transaction.
The lease, thus set up by the plaintiff has been
denied by the defendants who had pleaded that
the plaintiff had been entrusted with some
renovation work for which he was being paid and
the alleged document relied on by him was a
concocted one. The grant of mandatory injunction
would necessarily depend upon the plaintiff
establishing before the court that on 19.06.1998
when the court directed the parties to maintain
status quo, he was in possession as a tenant of
the plaint schedule property. The burden in that
behalf is clearly on the plaintiff, the claim he
made, having been denied by the defendants.
Therefore, the first question that the District Court
had to consider pursuant to the order of remand
by the High Court was whether the plaintiff had
prima facie established that the building was let
out to him as claimed. The building is seen to be
of a substantial dimension, within the District of
Howrah, part of a city, commercially important.
Prima facie it is difficult to imagine that such a
building or the second floor and part of the ground

16
floor of a building of this nature would have
been let out in such an informal manner and the
transaction not being evidenced even by a rent
deed executed by the lessor and the lessee in
terms of Section 107 of the Transfer of Property
Act. What the plaintiff has relied upon is seen to
be a letter on the letterhead of Khaitan Paper
Machine Limited signed by the first defendant
describing himself as Managing Director and
partner of Khaitan Estates. Prima facie it is
seen that whereas the letterhead is that of
Khaitan Paper Machine Limited, obviously a
limited company, the signature is that of the
Managing Director and partner of Khaitan
Estates, an entity different from Khaitan Paper
Machine Limited. It is difficult to imagine that
the letterhead of one company was used for
dealing with the properties of another entity
which appears to be a partnership as per the
description contained in the letter. Secondly the
letter purports to be an acknowledgement for
having received a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs as security
from the plaintiff and creating a tenancy in
favour of the plaintiff, and inducting the plaintiff
into possession in respect of the entire second
floor and shop rooms in the ground floor as a
tenant on a monthly rent of Rs. 7000 and
conferring upon the plaintiff a right to do certain
other acts in the premises. It is also stated that
a stamped agreement would be created by the
signatory as well as his wife, in favour of the
plaintiff. Prima facie, the document does not
satisfy the requirements of Section 107 of the
Transfer of Property Act and though it
acknowledges receipt of a sum of Rs. 2 lakhs,
there is no stamp affixed to indicate that it was
intended to be a receipt for the said sum. As
noticed, the rent stipulated is also Rs. 7000 per
month. Suffice it to notice, that the genuineness
of this document which is seriously disputed by
the defendants, its admissibility in evidence and
validity, have to be decided in the suit. Therefore,
one of the questions that has to be decided is
whether this letter is genuine and if it is
genuine, whether it is capable of bringing into
existence a lease or accepted as evidencing a lease
transaction between the parties. Since this is the
document on which the suit is based, the finding
on the genuineness and validity of this document
and the alleged transaction crated by it will have a
great bearing on the claim of possession by the

17
plaintiff. No doubt the signature of Defendant 1
found in the document is admitted but with an
explanation that it is a got-up document. A suit
has also been filed by the defendants
challenging it."
24) Learned counsel for defendant no. 2 /
respondent no. 2 would submit that the two
essential ingredients for granting injunction are - (i)
whether the appellants / plaintiffs are the owners of
the suit property and (ii) as to whether the
appellants / plaintiffs are in possession of the suit
property as on the date of filing of the suit. In
support of his contention reliance has been placed
on a decision rendered by Hon'ble Apex Court in
Anathula Sudhakar3. Paragraphs 13 to 16 of said
judgment are extracted hereunder:
"13. The general principles as to when a mere
suit for permanent injunction will lie, and when it is
necessary to file a suit for declaration and/or
possession with injunction as a consequential relief,
are well settled. We may refer to them briefly.
13.1. Where a plaintiff is in lawful or peaceful
possession of a property and such possession is
interfered or threatened by the defendant, a suit for an
injunction simpliciter will lie. A person has a right to
protect his possession against any person who does
not prove a better title by seeking a prohibitory
injunction. But a person in wrongful possession is not
entitled to an injunction against the rightful owner.
13.2. Where the title of the plaintiff is not
disputed, but he is not in possession, his remedy is to
file a suit for possession and seek in addition, if
necessary, an injunction. A person out of possession,
cannot seek the relief of injunction simpliciter, without
claiming the relief of possession.
13.3. Where the plaintiff is in possession, but
his title to the property is in dispute, or under a cloud,
or where the defendant asserts title thereto and there
is also a threat of dispossession from defendant, the
plaintiff will have to sue for declaration of title and the
consequential relief of injunction. Where the title of
plaintiff is under a cloud or in dispute and he is not in
possession or not able to establish possession,

18
necessarily the plaintiff will have to file a suit for
declaration, possession and injunction.
14. We may however clarify that a prayer for
declaration will be necessary only if the denial of title
by the defendant or challenge to plaintiff's title raises a
cloud on the title of plaintiff to the property. A cloud is
said to raise over a person's title, when some apparent
defect in his title to a property, or when some prima
facie right of a third party over it, is made out or
shown. An action for declaration, is the remedy to
remove the cloud on the title to the property. On the
other hand, where the plaintiff has clear title
supported by documents, if a trespasser without any
claim to title or an interloper without any apparent
title, merely denies the plaintiff's title, it does not
amount to raising a cloud over the title of the plaintiff
and it will not be necessary for the plaintiff to sue for
declaration and a suit for injunction may be sufficient.
Where the plaintiff, believing that defendant is only a
trespasser or a wrongful claimant without title, files a
mere suit for injunction, and in such a suit, the
defendant discloses in his defence the details of the
right or title claimed by him, which raises a serious
dispute or cloud over plaintiff's title, then there is a
need for the plaintiff, to amend the plaint and convert
the suit into one for declaration. Alternatively, he may
withdraw the suit for bare injunction, with permission
of the court to file a comprehensive suit for declaration
and injunction. He may file the suit for declaration
with consequential relief, even after the suit for
injunction is dismissed, where the suit raised only the
issue of possession and not any issue of title.
15. In a suit for permanent injunction to
restrain the defendant from interfering with plaintiff's
possession, the plaintiff will have to establish that as
on the date of the suit he was in lawful possession of
the suit property and defendant tried to interfere or
disturb such lawful possession. Where the property is
a building or building with appurtenant land, there
may not be much difficulty in establishing possession.
The plaintiff may prove physical or lawful possession,
either of himself or by him through his family
members or agents or lessees/licensees. Even in
respect of a land without structures, as for example an
agricultural land, possession may be established with
reference to the actual use and cultivation. The
question of title is not in issue in such a suit, though it
may arise incidentally or collaterally.
16. But what if the property is a vacant site,
which is not physically possessed, used or enjoyed? In
such cases the principle is that possession follows
title. If two persons claim to be in possession of a
vacant site, one who is able to establish title thereto
will be considered to be in possession, as against the

19
person who is not able to establish title. This means
that even though a suit relating to a vacant site is for a
mere injunction and the issue is one of possession, it
will be necessary to examine and determine the title as
a prelude for deciding the de jure possession. In such
a situation, where the title is clear and simple, the
court may venture a decision on the issue of title, so
as to decide the question of de jure possession even
though the suit is for a mere injunction. But where the
issue of title involves complicated or complex
questions of fact and law, or where court feels that
parties had not proceeded on the basis that title was at
issue, the court should not decide the issue of title in a
suit for injunction. The proper course is to relegate the
plaintiff to the remedy of a full-fledged suit for
declaration and consequential reliefs.
25) Learned counsel for defendant no. 2 /
respondent no. 2 would further submit that the
court below has rightly rejected the relief of
declaration and injunction sought by the plaintiffs
/ appellants as the injunction could not be issued
against the true owner. There is a dispute as to the
identification of the land. The plaintiffs' land as
claimed by them is Schedule A and B of the plaint
which is not the subject matter of agreement to sell
dated 27.02.2005. The Schedule A of the plaint
comprises of plot nos. 2363 to 2390, 2392 to 2400
and 2402 & 2403, admeasuring 26 acres. Schedule
B comprises of plot no. 2151 to 2153, 2155 to 2159,
2162 to 2170, 2172 & 2177, admeasuring 20 acres
whereof the subject matter of agreement to sell
dated 27.02.2005 is confined to khata no. 737
comprising of khasra no. 4595(k), 46589(c), 4688,
4689, 4687, 4690, 4691, 4692 etc. (31 plots)
admeasuring 10.0340 hectares. It is submitted that
suit for injunction was filed in relation to plots
mentioned in the agreement to sale and the
appellant / plaintiffs are not the owners of the land

20
in question. It is contended that agreement to sell
dated 27.02.2005 clearly shows how the property
has been transferred. The property was given by a
registered gift deed dated 20.08.1868 by Major
William James to Anglican Church, Diocese of
Lucknow. It is strongly contended that the land
mentioned in agreement to sell is different, there
can be no invasion on right of plaintiffs if any.
Sofar as entitlement of appellants / plaintiffs for
injunction with respect to suit property is
concerned, it is submitted that it is evident from a
perusal of the material on record that appellants /
plaintiffs have miserably failed to establish that the
land in question was ever possessed by them.
Meaning thereby, that appellant / plaintiff have not
proved to be the owner of disputed land. Therefore,
they are not entitled to get any relief as claimed.
Section 38 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963,
specifically states that an injunction restraining
disturbance of possession will not be granted in
favour of the plaintiff who is not found to be in
possession.
26) A perusal of the documents brought on
record would reveal that it has come in written
statement of defendant no. 2 that Lucknow Diocese
Trust Association is the owner of the suit property
as described in Schedule A and B of the plaint.
This fact has also come in the trust deed dated
24.12.1952. A further perusal of the General Power
of Attorney dated 30.01.1993 would depict that
properties situated within the jurisdiction of Diocese
of Agra still vest in Lucknow Diocese Trust

21
Association and has not been transferred to Agra
Diocesan Trust Association as yet. The plaintiffs on
the date of filing the suit claimed their title and
possession. However, they have filed a copy of the
trust deed dated 25.10.2008 and claimed the right
over the suit property through the said trust deed,
but the said deed does not confer any right or title
in favour of the plaintiffs. The trial court has
categorically recorded a finding that the name of the
plaintiff is not shown in the revenue records in
relation to the suit property. A further finding has
been recorded that plaintiff has not averred
anywhere that LDTA has no say in the formation of
Trust Deed dated 25.10.2008. Furthermore, in
support of the plaint, the plaintiffs / appellants
have only filed the photocopies and the same were
not proved in accordance with the provisions of the
Indian Evidence Act. In absence of proof of
documents, it can safely be presumed that the
plaintiffs / appellants utterly failed to prove the
existence and execution of the documents relied
upon by them. Photocopy of a document is neither
a primary evidence nor is it a secondary evidence.
An agreement to sell does not create any right or
title in favour of the intending buyer and transfer of
immoveable property by way of sale can be made by
a deed of conveyance of sale. Thus, it is abundantly
clear that as the cause of action has arisen on
27.02.2005, when agreement to sell was executed,
the plaintiffs have no real and genuine grievance.
The plaintiffs are duty bound to prove the certified
copy of the Trust deed dated 25.10.2008 as the
same is a public document. Therefore, when the

22
execution of Trust deed dated 25.10.2008 has not
been proved, the same is an inadmissible evidence
and no credence can be given to said document.

27) Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Ashok
Dulichand6 has held as under:
"After hearing the learned counsel for the
parties, we are of the opinion that the order of the
High Court in this respect calls for no interference.
According to clause (a) of section 65 of the Indian
Evidence Act, secondary evidence may be given of
the existence, condition or contents of a document
when the original is shown or appears to be in the
possession or power of the person against whom
the document is sought to be proved, or of any
person out of reach of, or not subject to, the
process of the Court, or of any person legally bound
to produce it, and when, after the notice mentioned
in section 66, such person does not produce it.
Clauses (b) to (g) of section 65 specify some other
contingencies wherein secondary evidence relating
to a document may be given, but we are not
concerned with those clauses as it is the common
case of the parties that the present case is not
covered by those clauses. In order to bring his case
within the purview of clause (a) of section 65, the
appellant filed applications on July 4, 1973, before
respondent No. 1 was examined as a witness,
praying that the said respondent be ordered to
produce the original manuscript of which,
according to the appellant, he had filed photostat
copy. Prayer was also made by the appellant that in
case respondent No. 1 denied that the said
manuscript had been written by him, the photostat
copy might be got examined from a handwriting
expert. The appellant also filed affidavit in support
of his applications. It was, however, nowhere stated
in the affidavit that the original document of which
the photostat copy had been filed by the appellant
was in the possession of respondent No. 1. There
was also no other material on the record to indicate
that the original document was in the possession of
respondent No. 1. The appellant further failed to
explain as to what were the circumstances under
which the photostat copy was prepared and who
was in possession of the original document at the
time its photograph was taken. Respondent No. 1
in his affidavit denied being in possession of or
having anything to do with such a document. The

23
photostat copy appeared to the High Court to be
not above suspicion. In view of all the
circumstances, the High Court came to the
conclusion that no foundation had been laid by the
appellant for leading secondary evidence in the
shape of the photostat copy. We find no infirmity in
the above order of the High Court as might justify
interference by this Court."
28) Their Lordships of Hon'ble Apex Court in
Rakesh Mohindra2 have held as under:
 "20. It is well settled that if a party wishes
to lead secondary evidence, the court is obliged to
examine the probative value of the document
produced in the court or their contents and decide
the question of admissibility of a document in
secondary evidence. At the same time, the party
has to lay down the factual foundation to establish
the right to give secondary evidence where the
original document cannot be produced. It is
equally well settled that neither mere admission of
a document in evidence amounts to its proof nor
mere making of an exhibit of a document dispense
with its proof, which is otherwise required to be
done in accordance with law."
29) In Smt. J. Yashoda4, it has been held by the
Hon'ble Supreme Court as under:
 "7. Secondary evidence, as a general rule,
is admissible only in the absence of primary
evidence. If the original itself is found to be
inadmissible through failure of the party who files
it to prove it to be valid, the same party is not
entitled to introduce secondary evidence of its
contents.
 8. Essentially, secondary evidence is an
evidence which may be given in the absence of that
better evidence which law requires to be given first,
when a proper explanation of its absence is given.
The definition in Section 63 is exhaustive as the
Section declares that secondary evidence "means
and includes" and then follow the five kinds of
secondary evidence.
 9. The rule which is the most universal
namely that the best evidence the nature of the
case will admit shall be produced, decides this
objection that rule only means that, so long as the
higher or superior evidence is within your
possession or may be reached by you, you shall
give no inferior proof in relation to it. Section 65

24
deals with the proof of the contents of the
document tendered in evidence. In order to enable
a party to produce secondary evidence it is
necessary for the party to prove existence and
execution of the original document. Under Section
64, documents are to be provided by primary
evidence. Section 65, however, permits secondary
evidence to be given of the existence, condition or
contents of documents under the circumstances
mentioned. The conditions laid down in the said
Section must be fulfilled before secondary evidence
can be admitted. Secondary evidence of the
contents of a document cannot be admitted without
non-production of the original being first accounted
for in such a manner as to bring it within one or
other or the cases provided for in the Section...."
30) Admittedly, the property in respect of
which the agreement dated 27.02.2005 has been
executed is an agricultural land. Present suit seeking
permanent injunction has been filed on account of
ownership and title in the suit property. However, the
plaintiffs upon whom the burden of proof lies in view
of Section 101 of Indian Evidence Act failed to
produce any document pertaining to title in the suit
property. It is evident that the entire documentary
evidence filed by the plaintiffs are the photocopies
which are not admissible in evidence. Moreover, on
the date of filing of the suit in respect of an
agricultural land, the name of the plaintiffs was not
even recorded in revenue records, therefore, the suit
seeking injunction in respect of an agricultural land
has been instituted without plaintiffs being recorded
in the revenue records.
31) Plaintiffs have utterly failed to prove by
pleading or by adducing evidence that they are the
owners in possession of the suit property. Any
immoveable property could only be transferred by way
of sale, gift or by virtue of a Will and any document

25
creating, vesting or transferring right in respect of any
immoveable property necessarily requires registration
and should be filed in original being the basis of the
suit. Here the plaintiffs / appellants had failed to
discharge the burden of proof while seeking injunction
against the defendants.
32) Indisputably, the suit property is an
agricultural land and the plaintiffs are not the
recorded owners of the suit property. Thus the
question of declaration is also involved, which a civil
court cannot grant to the plaintiffs as the decree of
declaration only can be passed by the competent
court having revenue jurisdiction. There is no
illegality or perversity in the impugned judgment and
decree passed by the trial court while dismissing the
suit for permanent injunction. It is settled position in
law that the plaintiff has to succeed on its own
strength and he cannot succeed on the weakness of
the defendant. The point of determination / issue
involved in the appeal is answered accordingly.
33) In view of the foregoing discussion, the first
appeal is devoid of merit and is liable to be dismissed.
The same is hereby dismissed. Interim order dated
27.04.2016, passed by this Court, is hereby vacated.
34) In the facts and circumstances of the case
there will be no order as to costs.
